items.title: Agriculture — Systems, Seasons & Cropping Patterns
items.body:
## Farming systems

| System | Feature | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Primitive subsistence | Slash-and-burn, low inputs | Podu (AP), Jhumming (NE), Dipa (Chhattisgarh) |
| Intensive subsistence | Labour-intensive, small plots, high population pressure | WB, UP, Bihar, Punjab, TN |
| Commercial | HYV seeds, fertilisers, market-oriented | Punjab/Haryana rice & wheat |
| Plantation | Single crop, capital-intensive, industrial raw material | Tea (Assam), coffee (Karnataka), rubber (Kerala) |

- The **same crop** can be commercial in one region and subsistence in another — e.g. rice in Punjab (commercial) vs Odisha (subsistence).

## Cropping seasons

- **Kharif** (Jun–Sep, monsoon): rice, cotton, jute, groundnut, pulses.
- **Rabi** (Oct–Mar, winter): wheat, gram, mustard, barley.
- **Zaid** (Mar/Apr–Jun/Jul, summer): watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables.

## Green Revolution & land use

- The 1960s **Green Revolution** introduced HYVs, chiefly boosting **wheat** (a rabi crop) in irrigated Punjab-Haryana-western UP, creating regional disparity.
- Total geographical area ~328.8 m ha; net sown area ~143 m ha.
keyPoints: Shifting cultivation is called Podu in Andhra Pradesh and Jhumming in the north-east.
Kharif = June-September monsoon crops (rice, cotton); Rabi = winter crops (wheat, gram); Zaid = short summer crops.
Plantation crops: tea (Assam), coffee (Karnataka), rubber (Kerala) — single crop, industrial raw material.
Rice is commercial in Punjab/Haryana but subsistence in Odisha.
The 1960s Green Revolution mainly raised wheat output in irrigated north-west India.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Geography: Agriculture; Major Crops of India

items.title: Major Crops & Agricultural Revolutions
items.body:
## Leading producer states

| Crop | No.1 state | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Rice | West Bengal | India 2nd after China; staple |
| Wheat | Uttar Pradesh | India 2nd after China |
| Sugarcane | Uttar Pradesh | India 2nd after Brazil |
| Cotton | Gujarat | black soil of Deccan; kharif |
| Jute | West Bengal | 'golden fibre'; India largest producer |
| Tea | Assam | India 2nd producer |
| Coffee | Karnataka | Arabica; Baba Budan Hills |
| Rubber | Kerala | equatorial crop |
| Pulses | Madhya Pradesh | India largest producer & consumer |
| Millets | Rajasthan | nutri-cereals |

- **Groundnut** is a kharif crop and ~half of India's oilseeds; **linseed & mustard** are rabi.
- Pulses (except arhar) **fix nitrogen**, restoring soil fertility.

## Agricultural revolutions

| Revolution | Sector |
|---|---|
| Green | Foodgrains (wheat, rice) |
| White (Operation Flood) | Milk |
| Yellow | Oilseeds |
| Blue | Fisheries |
| Golden | Horticulture/fruits |
| Golden Fibre | Jute |
| Silver Fibre | Cotton |
keyPoints: Rice leader = West Bengal; Wheat & Sugarcane leader = Uttar Pradesh; Cotton = Gujarat; Jute = West Bengal.
Coffee (Karnataka) is Arabica, introduced on Baba Budan Hills; tea leader is Assam.
India is the world's largest producer and consumer of pulses; leader Madhya Pradesh.
White = milk, Yellow = oilseeds, Blue = fisheries, Golden Fibre = jute, Silver Fibre = cotton.
Groundnut is a kharif crop making up ~half of India's oilseeds.

items.title: Mineral Resources — Metallic, Non-Metallic & Fuels
items.body:
## Metallic minerals

| Mineral | Leading state(s) | Key locations |
|---|---|---|
| Iron ore | Odisha | Bailadila (Chhattisgarh), Ballari (Karnataka) |
| Manganese | Odisha | Nagpur-Bhandara (Maharashtra) |
| Chromite | Odisha | Sukinda Valley |
| Bauxite | Odisha | Koraput; feeds aluminium |
| Copper | Madhya Pradesh | Malanjkhand (largest), Khetri (Rajasthan) |
| Gold | Karnataka | Kolar, Hutti; Ramagiri (AP) |

- Iron-ore grades: **Hematite (~70%) > Magnetite (60–70%) > Limonite > Siderite**.

## Non-metallic minerals

- **Mica**: AP is the largest producer (Gudur); Koderma (Jharkhand) = 'Mica Capital'.
- **Limestone**: Rajasthan leads; feeds cement; AP reserves in Kadapa/Kurnool.
- **Barytes**: **Mangampeta (Kadapa, AP)** — among the world's largest deposits.
- **Diamond**: Panna (Madhya Pradesh) — India's only operational diamond mine.

## Fossil fuels

- **Coal**: Gondwana fields (Damodar, Mahanadi, Godavari–Singareni) + Tertiary (NE); ~70% of electricity.
- **Petroleum**: Mumbai High (offshore, 1973), Gujarat, Assam (Digboi — first refinery 1901), KG & Cauvery basins, Barmer.
- **Natural gas**: KG basin, Mumbai High; **GAIL** (1984) is the largest gas PSU (Maharatna).
keyPoints: Odisha leads iron ore, manganese, chromite (Sukinda) and bauxite (Koraput).
Hematite (~70% Fe) is the highest-grade iron ore; Bailadila mines are in Chhattisgarh.
Copper largest mine Malanjkhand (MP); mica largest producer Andhra Pradesh (Gudur).
Mangampeta (Kadapa, AP) is among the world's largest barytes deposits.
Damodar Valley holds Raniganj/Jharia/Bokaro; coal supplies ~70% of India's power.
Mumbai High (offshore, 1973) and the Krishna-Godavari basin are major hydrocarbon provinces.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Geography: Mineral Resources — Metallic, Non-Metallic, Coal/Petroleum/Natural Gas

items.title: Energy Resources — Thermal, Hydro, Nuclear & Renewables
items.body:
## Conventional vs non-conventional

- **Conventional**: coal, petroleum, natural gas, nuclear — finite, higher pollution.
- **Non-conventional (renewable)**: solar, wind, hydro, biogas, geothermal, tidal — clean, replenishable.

## Thermal & hydro

- Coal-fired thermal plants supply ~**75%** of electricity; located near coalfields/load centres (~3–4 ha/MW).
- Largest thermal: **Vindhyachal (MP, 4,760 MW)**.
- India ranks **5th** globally in hydro; oldest station **Shivanasamudra (Karnataka, 1902)**; **Tehri (Uttarakhand)** highest dam.
- AP: **Simhadri** (thermal), **Srisailam** & **Nagarjunasagar** (hydro).

## Nuclear — Bhabha's three-stage programme

1. **Stage 1**: PHWR, natural uranium → plutonium-239.
2. **Stage 2**: Fast Breeder Reactors using plutonium.
3. **Stage 3**: Thorium-based reactors (uranium-233) — for India's abundant thorium (Kerala monazite).
- First plant **Tarapur**; Apsara (1956) was Asia's first reactor; NPCIL operates the plants; AERB regulates.

## Renewables

- **Bhadla (Rajasthan, ~2,245 MW)** = world's largest solar park; **Kurnool (AP, 1,000 MW)**.
- Wind: Tamil Nadu (Muppandal), Rajasthan (Jaisalmer); India is a top-4 wind producer.
- Target: **500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030**; National Solar Mission (2010).
keyPoints: Thermal (coal) plants supply ~75% of India's electricity; India ranks 5th in hydropower.
Bhabha's three-stage programme: PHWR (uranium) -> Fast Breeder -> Thorium reactors.
India has limited uranium (Jaduguda) but abundant thorium in Kerala's monazite sands.
Bhadla (Rajasthan) is the world's largest solar park; Kurnool is a major AP solar park.
India targets 500 GW non-fossil-fuel capacity by 2030.
AP power projects: Simhadri (thermal), Srisailam & Nagarjunasagar (hydro).

items.title: Transport — Railways, Roadways, Ports & Waterways
items.body:
## Railways

- 4th-largest network; **18 zones**; the newest **South Coast Railway** is headquartered at **Visakhapatnam**.
- Gauges: **Broad 1,676 mm**, Metre 1,000 mm, Narrow 762 mm.
- First train: **Mumbai–Thane, 1853**. Dedicated Freight Corridors (Eastern & Western) ease freight.
- **Golden Quadrilateral** (rail & road) links Delhi–Mumbai–Chennai–Kolkata.

## Roadways

- **National Highways** (NHAI): ~2% of length but ~40% of traffic; **NH-44** (Srinagar–Kanyakumari) is the longest.
- Then State Highways, District, Village (**PMGSY** rural), Border (**BRO**) roads.
- **Bharatmala Pariyojana** — highway/economic-corridor programme.

## Ports & waterways

- **13 major ports** (Union) + 200+ minor ports handle 90%+ of trade by volume.
- Kolkata = oldest; **JNPT (Nhava Sheva)** = largest container port; **Visakhapatnam** = AP's only major port.
- **National Waterways**: NW-1 Ganga (1,620 km, longest), NW-2 Brahmaputra, NW-3 West Coast Canal, NW-4 Krishna-Godavari-Buckingham (through AP), NW-5 Brahmani-Mahanadi.
- **Sagarmala** = port-led development; **Jal Marg Vikas** develops NW-1.
keyPoints: Indian Railways has 18 zones; South Coast Railway (newest) HQ is at Visakhapatnam.
Broad gauge = 1,676 mm; India's first train ran Mumbai-Thane in 1853.
NH-44 (Srinagar-Kanyakumari) is India's longest national highway; NHs carry ~40% of traffic.
India has 13 major ports; JNPT is the largest container port and Kolkata the oldest.
NW-1 (Ganga, 1,620 km) is the longest national waterway; NW-4 passes through Andhra Pradesh.
Sagarmala drives port-led development; Bharatmala develops highways.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Geography: Transport — Railways, Roadways, Waterways

items.title: Economic Geography of Andhra Pradesh & Sobriquets
items.body:
## Andhra Pradesh — economic geography

- **Coastline** ~974 km — the longest on India's east coast — underpins fisheries, ports and aquaculture.
- **Ports**: Visakhapatnam (only major/Union port; deep natural harbour), plus deep-water/State ports **Gangavaram** and **Krishnapatnam**, and the developing **Machilipatnam** and new greenfield ports (Ramayapatnam, Bhavanapadu).
- **Deltaic agriculture**: the **Godavari and Krishna deltas** are 'rice bowls'; AP leads India in **shrimp/marine-product exports** (aquaculture).
- **Industrial corridor**: the **Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor (VCIC)** — part of the ADB-backed East Coast Economic Corridor.
- **Minerals**: barytes (Mangampeta, world-class), limestone (Kadapa/Kurnool), mica (Gudur), heavy mineral sands.
- **Power**: Simhadri thermal; Srisailam & Nagarjunasagar hydro; Kurnool Ultra Mega Solar Park.

## Sobriquets (geographical nicknames)

| Sobriquet | Place |
|---|---|
| City of Destiny | Visakhapatnam |
| Manchester of India | Ahmedabad |
| Steel City / Pittsburgh of India | Jamshedpur |
| Queen of the Arabian Sea | Kochi |
| Land of Black Diamond | Asansol |
| Roof of the World | Pamir Plateau |
| Land of Rising Sun | Japan |
| Dark Continent | Africa |
keyPoints: AP's ~974 km east coastline is India's longest peninsular east coast; drives ports and aquaculture.
Visakhapatnam is AP's only major port; Gangavaram and Krishnapatnam are deep-water ports.
The Godavari and Krishna deltas are AP's rice bowls; AP leads India in shrimp exports.
VCIC (Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor) is part of the East Coast Economic Corridor.
Visakhapatnam's sobriquet is 'City of Destiny'; Ahmedabad = 'Manchester of India'.
Mangampeta (Kadapa) barytes is a world-class AP mineral deposit.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Geography: Transport — Waterways; Sobriquet; Mineral Resources; regional economic facts

items.title: World Agricultural & Industrial Regions and Mineral Producers
items.body:
## World agricultural regions (Whittlesey types)

| System | Region | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Extensive commercial grain (wheat) | Prairies, Steppes, Pampas, Downs, Canadian Prairies | Highly mechanised; great wheat belts |
| Corn Belt / mixed farming | US Midwest; temperate Europe | Crops + livestock |
| Intensive wet-rice (subsistence) | Monsoon Asia | High labour, high population pressure |
| Plantation | Tropics | Tea, rubber, coffee, cocoa, sugarcane |
| Mediterranean | Med basin, California, Chile, Cape, S/SW Australia | Citrus, vine, olive |
| Dairy farming | NW Europe, NE USA, New Zealand | Near markets/cool moist climate |
| Livestock ranching | Pampas, Prairies, Australian Downs, veld | Extensive grazing |

- Temperate grasslands are the world's 'granaries' and great ranching lands.

## World major industrial regions

| Region | Feature |
|---|---|
| Ruhr (Germany) | Coal & steel |
| North American Manufacturing Belt | Great Lakes-NE USA heavy industry |
| Kanto (Tokyo-Yokohama) & Kansai (Osaka-Kobe), Japan | Diversified manufacturing |
| Lancashire (UK) | Cotton textiles |
| Donbas (Ukraine) | Coal & steel |

- Heavy industry clusters near coalfields, iron ore and navigable water/ports.

## Leading world producers of minerals & energy

| Resource | Largest producer | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Iron ore | Australia | Pilbara; Brazil's Carajas = high-grade hematite |
| Copper | Chile | Escondida mine, Atacama |
| Coal | China | >50% of world output; USA largest reserves |
| Crude oil | USA (output) | Venezuela largest reserves; Ghawar largest field |
| Natural gas | USA | Russia largest reserves; Qatar top LNG exporter |
| Uranium | Kazakhstan | Australia largest reserves |
| Diamonds | Russia (volume) | Botswana leads by value |
| Gold | China | Australia largest reserves |
keyPoints: Temperate grasslands (Prairies, Steppes, Pampas, Downs) are the world's great wheat and ranching belts; monsoon Asia is the wet-rice region.
Plantation agriculture (tea/rubber/coffee) is tropical; Mediterranean agriculture means citrus, vine and olive.
Ruhr (Germany) = coal & steel; North American Manufacturing Belt = Great Lakes-NE USA; Kanto = Japan's Tokyo-Yokohama belt; Lancashire = UK cotton textiles.
Australia leads iron-ore production (Pilbara); Chile leads copper (Escondida); China leads coal.
Kazakhstan is the largest uranium producer; Australia has the largest uranium and gold reserves.
Venezuela holds the largest crude-oil reserves; Russia the largest natural-gas reserves; Botswana leads diamonds by value, Russia by volume.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — World Geography: Mineral and Energy Resources; NCERT/Goh Cheng Leong — Certificate Physical & Human Geography (agricultural & industrial regions)

items.title: Fishing Grounds, Industrial Location, Coal Types & Agro-Inputs
items.body:
## World fishing grounds

- The great fishing grounds lie where **warm and cold ocean currents meet** (e.g. Grand Banks — Labrador + Gulf Stream), over **broad continental shelves**, and in **upwelling** zones — all rich in plankton.

## Industrial location

- **Weber's least-cost theory**: industry locates to minimise transport + labour costs. **Weight-losing, raw-material-oriented** industries (iron & steel) sit near coal/iron (**Chhota Nagpur**); **market/labour-oriented** industries (cotton textiles) locate near markets (Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Coimbatore); **sugar** is cane-belt (raw-material) oriented.

## Coal — Gondwana vs Tertiary

| Type | Age | Rank | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Gondwana** (~98%) | ~250 mya | Bituminous | Damodar (Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro), Godavari (**Singareni**), Mahanadi, Son valleys |
| **Tertiary** | ~15–60 mya | **Lignite** (brown coal) | **Neyveli (Tamil Nadu)**; also NE India, Kashmir, Rajasthan |

## Agro-inputs & crop use

- **Neem-coated urea** is promoted because it **slows the rate of dissolution of urea in soil**, improving nitrogen-use efficiency and curbing diversion to industry.
- **Maize** is used for **starch, biodiesel feedstock and alcoholic beverages** — a versatile agro-industrial crop.
- **Heavy/inappropriate sand-mining** in riverbeds lowers the water table, damages river ecology and increases bank erosion — a resource-extraction externality.
keyPoints: Great fishing grounds occur where warm and cold currents meet, over broad continental shelves and in upwelling zones.
Weber's least-cost theory: raw-material-oriented industries (iron & steel) locate near inputs; market/labour-oriented (cotton textiles) near markets.
About 98% of India's coal is Gondwana (bituminous) in Damodar/Godavari/Mahanadi/Son valleys; Singareni is in the Godavari valley.
Tertiary coal is lignite (brown coal); Neyveli (Tamil Nadu) is the main lignite field.
Neem-coated urea slows urea dissolution in soil, improving nitrogen-use efficiency.
Maize is used for starch, biodiesel feedstock and alcoholic beverages.
Excessive riverbed sand-mining lowers water tables and increases bank erosion.
